To us Jesus is the Christ who stood condemned before lawful authority and was right. When an imperial judge sat down at Carthage and courteously offered our bishops chairs, our own bishop of Constantina thanked him and refused. Two hundred and seventy-nine of us had answered the roll that morning, and our bishops stood for three days. That is the Christ we carried: the one who was tried, who lost his case in the eyes of the power judging him, and who was vindicated not by that power's reversal but by God's own act afterward.

We confessed him in the same Latin words as our opponents — the Son, one God with the Father and the Spirit, who died and was raised. For most of a century the charge against us was schism, not heresy, because both sides said the same creed. The quarrel was never about who Christ is. It was about who may hand on what he gave.

His death meant that the end of a faithful life is not an interruption of it. Our own martyr was shown a cup, a crown and a palm four days before he was thrown from a cliff — shown, in advance, what finishing looked like. And a bishop writing to his own congregation about two of their number tortured to death closed by telling them plainly that the same might yet be asked of any of them. That is our gospel in its working form: he stood, he was condemned, he was raised, and the day they come for you is not the day it all went wrong.

The books reached us through Africa, and through Carthage, in Latin, in the line of Cyprian - our own bishop and our own martyr, half a century before the persecution that made us. His letters and his councils were ours before they were anyone else's. We did not think we had received the faith from Rome, and we did not think we needed Rome to keep it.

What we had about Jesus was books. That is not a figure of speech with us - it is the whole of our history. When the persecution opened, the emperor's edict demanded that the scriptures be handed over and burned, along with the vessels of the church. Some of our clergy carried the codices out and gave them up. Others refused and paid for refusing. We are the church that came out of that difference, and we have never stopped naming it. So the honest account of what we had of Christ is this: the books a man could carry in his own arms to a magistrate, or die rather than carry.

None of us had known someone who saw him. Three hundred years stood between us and that, and we never pretended otherwise. We did not argue from a chain of eyewitnesses at all. We argued from a chain of hands - whose hands ordained whose, back to a point where the line was still clean.

We will not pretend this is a question we ever wrote an answer to. Not one line survives from any of us on what to say to someone who could not believe. What we can tell you is what we actually did when someone came. We did not examine the person coming. We examined the hand. For what we look to is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient - our own bishop's own words: “What we look for is the conscience of the giver - the one who gives in holiness - to cleanse that of the recipient. Someone who knowingly takes faith from the faithless receives not faith, but guilt.”. Whatever you have done, it was never your record that was on trial at our font. It was ours.

That means we cannot hand you a sentence we would have said to you in the room where you named your struggle. We can only tell you what the crossing itself was like. Coming to believe among us was not a private settling of the mind. It was a public act with a date on it, and everyone in the street knew which way you had walked. You walked to one font and not the other, and you chose which set of hands went into the water with you. The door was wider than our reputation. Our own council took back clergy it had condemned in the harshest words it owned, without repeating anything. So the line was not where our hardest language put it.

Whether an ordinary member of ours, on an ordinary evening, could feel nothing and wonder whether it was all a mistake - we cannot tell you. That is not modesty. It is that fear, wavering and quiet leaving are exactly what a record kept by our enemies does not preserve. What survives of our inner weather is vindication and defiance, and it survives because it sits in the martyr texts nobody edited.

We held the same creed as the church we spent a century fighting: Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God, in the same Latin words they said it. For most of a century the charge against us was schism, not heresy, because both sides confessed the identical faith. By about 400 the bishop of Hippo was calling us heretics, and he said why: our separation made us so. The emperor's law of 405 then placed us beside the Manichaeans. Yet in 417 that same bishop wrote that we held one substance in the Trinity, and that most of us declared the same faith as his church. He wrote that this was never the question in dispute, and that we ourselves denied being heretics. Two churches stood in every African town reciting the same faith at each other. That is precisely what made the fight unbearable: there was no doctrinal difference to point at, only the question of who had the right to say the words at all.

On what we believed about God, we are poorer than you would expect. We were not a teaching movement. We can show you no school, no system, no line of doctors. Only one book of interpretation survives, by a layman named Tyconius, and our own council condemned him. Our councils decided who might stand at an altar, not what might be said about the Godhead.

We held the same confession of God as the church we fought. Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God - not three gods, not a Father above a lesser Son, but one divine being in three persons. We spoke it in the same Latin words they did, creed for creed, and for most of a century the charge against us was schism, not heresy, because the confession was identical.

Our councils met to settle who the true church is, not to argue what God is. The great eastern councils of that century - Nicaea, Constantinople - do not appear in our own record. We were not absent from those fights because we held a different doctrine. We were absent because our fight was elsewhere: in every African town where two bishops stood, two altars, two baptismal fonts, reciting the same creed and disputing whose hand could be trusted to give what that creed promised.

What shaped how we spoke of God was not speculative theology. It was this: we are the Church of the Martyrs. The pure, persecuted, true church, and what we have suffered proves the claim is held sincerely rather than asserted for advantage. So when we said God, we meant the God who sees that difference - between a church that suffers for refusing to concede the truth and a church that enjoys the emperor's favor for accepting a settlement we will not accept. Our dead are held by name, at the grave, on the appointed day, their accounts read aloud. We said the same creed our opponents did. We said it standing in a different place.

Beyond that, we wrote almost nothing. We produced no school of theology, no body of doctors arguing the nature of God at length. One man among us, Tyconius, wrote seven rules for reading Scripture rightly, and it is the strongest theological work our people ever produced - and his own council condemned him for it. We put everything we had into one question: whose hand may give what the church gives. We had nothing left over for the rest.

A council of bishops decided, and among us that was never a formality. Our councils deposed men, restored men, and shut down a rival primate. Three hundred and ten of our bishops sat at Bagai and condemned a breakaway party in one sentence, and the same body later took two of the condemned back into office. That is not an advisory board. That is a church governing itself.

But here is what we cannot show you. On matters of doctrine, we have almost nothing. The great eastern councils of that century are not our fight and do not appear in our record. Every council our own bishops sat in was about one question — who the true church is — and none of them was about who Christ is. We were not a teaching movement. We can show you no school, no system, no line of doctors — only one book of interpretation, by one man. Tyconius, a layman of ours, wrote seven rules for reading scripture. It is the one wholly original work of interpretation we produced. Our own council then condemned him, and he gathered almost no following. So yes, a council could settle a dispute — by telling a man to stop. What we cannot hand you is the council making doctrine rather than disciplining the man who made it.

Your question reaches a place where we have to be honest about what we cannot show you. We split forgiveness in two, and that much is ours to say. Whether a man was pardoned was never the fight we were in. The fight was whether his hand could still give what he claimed to give. So a man might be forgiven, by God or by the people he had failed, and still be a man who could no longer ordain, because those are two different questions and our doctrine only ever answered the second. We would say that is not bitterness. It is keeping two separate accounts separate.

But you are asking about struggle, not about judgment. What we offered a person whose own mind would not go quiet, we cannot tell you. Whether we knew the silence of praying and hearing nothing back, we cannot tell you that either. Not one of us left a word on either. It is not that our people had no inner life. It is that what survives of us was kept by people arguing with us, and a man arguing with you does not write down your bad nights.

What we can show you is the public threshold and the public consequences. If you came to us from the other communion, we put you in the water. The thing being examined at our font was never your record. It was the record of the man standing in the water with you. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked. And we know that not every hand that went under our water chose to be there. Many of our own people did not want the water repeated. That much reaches us through our opponents' own argument, which means it is likely true. But what those people felt before or after, or whether they stayed or left quietly, or what a person who struggled to believe found among us — that is exactly what a hostile record does not preserve.

We read our scriptures combatively, and about one subject. On the third day at Carthage the bishop of Hippo argued from the wheat and the tares that a church holds good and bad together, and that what is to be saved is the world. Our own bishop of Caesarea answered him out of the same books, verse against verse - the world did not know him; every mouth stopped and all guilty before God; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you; if any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. That is our reading in one exchange. We went to the text for a test of which of two visible churches was the true one, and we found the church described as the party the world hates rather than the party it favours.

We will not pretend that was a method. It was not. One man among us built an actual system for reading - seven rules, worked out and written down - and our own leadership told him to stop preaching what they led to, and cut him off. His book survives; we can show you no one who followed him. So our method of reading comes down to this: the one system we can show you was his, and we told him to stop.

A modern reader would miss that we were not reading for comfort or for doctrine. We were reading for a test we could apply on a Tuesday, in a street, to two buildings. Your town has two bishops. Both recite the same creed. Both call their building the church. One of them has the emperor's letter and the magistrate's protection, and one does not. You have to choose, and no article of faith will separate them for you, because they hold the same articles. So you go looking in the text for something that will separate them - some mark that can be seen from outside. The true church is the one being hated. Look at which of the two doors the soldiers are standing outside, and you have your answer.

We cannot give you a list of the books we treated as scripture. Nothing that survives from us settles it, and we would rather say so than hand you the canon of some other church and put our name on it.

Almost none of it would survive the way a modern scholar measures these things, and we will tell you why.

Nearly every page of our own history passes through the hands of two men who were writing to refute us. Our best theologian's letters survive chopped into clauses inside the book built to demolish them. The fullest account of our founding decade is a polemic aimed at proving us wrong. So when you hear us tell a story with rich detail, the right question is whether the detail is ours or the detail of a man who needed it to land a blow.

But the founding documents run the other way, and they do not flatter us. There is a court transcript in which a notary confesses, under threat of torture, that he forged the letter proving our central accusation - and that he did it working for our side. There is another in which our own bishops are read out advising each other, in writing, to keep a charge out of court because it was true. We could not remove those if we wanted to. They are the most checkable things we have, and they are the worst things about us.

And there is one thing nobody mediated at all. On two pillars near Bagai, and on three other stones, two words are cut: Deo laudes. Praise to God. That is our own voice with no enemy standing between you and it, and it is two words long. We know our own shout better than we know the room we shouted it in.

Our record is thinnest wherever it could be checked without a hostile hand. The inner life of any ordinary member. The words of any woman among us. The rooms we met in. Our own account of any of the councils that judged us. And a whole shelf of modern work on us that this telling has not read.

We held the same scriptures, recited the same creed, called on the same Lord. So the reading could not settle who was right by discovering a doctrine one side held and the other denied. It had to do something else. It had to give you a mark you could see from outside, standing in a street, looking at two buildings.

Your town has two bishops. Both call their building the church. One of them has the emperor's letter and the magistrate's protection. One does not. You have to choose, and no article of faith will separate them for you, because they hold the same articles. So you go looking in the text for something that will separate them - some mark that can be seen from outside.

That is what our own bishop of Caesarea was doing when he answered the bishop of Hippo verse against verse: the world did not know him; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you; if any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. In your hands those may be verses about the soul's detachment. In ours they were an identification mark. The true church is the one being hated. Look at which of the two doors the soldiers are standing outside, and you have your answer.

A modern reader misses something smaller too. Two words could carry all of this. Where they said thanks to God, we said praise to God - Deo laudes - and we cut it into stone. A great deal of our reading works like that: not the discovery of a hidden sense, but a plain sentence turned into a badge you could be identified by.

We would not put the claim where you have put it. We never argued that our practice came down from the apostles in an unbroken chain of custom. We argued something narrower and, we thought, harder to dodge: that it came down from Carthage.

Half a century before there was any quarrel between us and the other party, eighty-seven African bishops sat in council at Carthage under Cyprian, and ruled that what is given outside the true church is not given at all - so anyone coming in from outside is baptized, not re-baptized. That is not our invention. That is the settled mind of the African church before either of our two hierarchies existed. When our opponents told us we had made something up in the year of Caecilian's consecration, our answer was that we had changed nothing, and they had. We were holding the old African position; they had moved off it to keep the peace with Rome.

You can measure how much that argument weighed by how hard it had to be answered. Seven books were written against our practice of washing, and a great part of that labour goes on explaining that Cyprian, however holy, is not a canonical authority - that the Scriptures alone are, and that Cyprian's own real lesson was to stay in unity anyway. Nobody spends that many pages on a father unless the appeal to him is doing damage.

Here is the honest end of it. Cyprian ruled as we ruled and did not do what we did. He never broke communion over it. That is the strongest thing our opponents had, and we would not pretend it is weak. And beyond him we cannot take you. We can show you an African council in the middle of the third century. We cannot show you the apostles.

Among us, leadership was established through the people and the bishops together, and it ran through a whole rival church built see for see against our opponents. From the outset there were two rival bishoprics at Carthage, and the contest was repeated town for town across Africa. At the great Conference in 411, two hundred and seventy-nine of our bishops stood against two hundred and eighty-six of theirs — that is not a movement, it is one whole church facing another.

A man came to hold that authority through the people and the bishops together, and here is what that looked like when it went wrong. At Cirta, when Silvanus was being made bishop, the people shouted back — let it be another; hear us, God — and he was made bishop anyway, and a court heard about it years later from a man who said, I myself fought against his being made bishop. So a crowd could be overridden, but it could not be ignored.

Our senior bishop sat at Carthage. Donatus held it, then Parmenian, then Primian. Our rival claimed the same see for its own man at the same time, so there were two primates in one city, as there were two bishops in every town.

Councils held the bishops, and among us that was never a formality. Our councils deposed men, restored men, and shut down a rival primate. Three hundred and ten of our bishops sat at Bagai and condemned a breakaway party in one sentence, and the same body later took two of the condemned back into office. That is not an advisory board — that is a church governing itself.

But we have to answer crookedly about one thing: whether a woman could carry real authority among us, because no woman among us left a line. Here is what we can show. The whole founding story, as our enemies tell it, turns on a wealthy laywoman of Carthage — her fortune, her household, her grievance. In their telling she made a bishop. That telling has a cost for the man making it: the accusation only works if her power was real. A hostile source that needs a woman's agency in order to blame her has recorded that agency, whatever it meant to do. What it cost her we do not know, except that it cost her this: she is the reason a whole church was said to exist, and she does not get to speak once in her own defence. There was a second woman too, behind the later breakaway at Cebarsussi, whom the same hand parallels to her and never names at all.

No. That is the wrong picture entirely, and we need to name why. Nobody among us hid underground. The persecutions of our own years did not send us into tunnels. They sent soldiers into our buildings in daylight, under orders, to enforce one church. We read the account of one such day aloud every year: a basilica at Carthage seized, a house of prayer turned into a place of feasting and licence, people clubbed to death where they knelt with their eyes shut, and buried inside the walls because there was nowhere else and nobody to stop it. That is what persecution looked like for us. Not hiding. Being visited.

The catacombs belong to an earlier century and a different persecution entirely. By our own years, the question was not whether a Christian could meet openly. It was which of two openly meeting churches the state would recognise as lawful. We had bishops, basilicas, and councils large enough to be governments. What we did not have was the emperor's favour. That is a different kind of danger, and it never once drove us into tunnels.

The two-party contest itself did not end at the 411 Conference. It persisted under Vandal and then Byzantine rule for roughly a further century and a half. Then the record simply stops. No line runs from us to any communion you could walk into now.

If you came to us from the other communion, we put you in the water. That is the step, and everything else follows from it. We would not call it a second baptism; on our reckoning you have not had a first. A hand out of a line that broke has nothing in it to hand over. What we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient: “What we look for is the conscience of the giver - the one who gives in holiness - to cleanse that of the recipient. Someone who knowingly takes faith from the faithless receives not faith, but guilt.”

So the thing being examined at our font was never your record. It was the record of the man standing in the water with you. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked.

It happened once, bodily, on a day, and the town knew. There was no quiet way to do it. Imperial edicts name the practice specifically, which tells you how public it was: washing a Catholic again was the plainest possible refusal of the settlement the state was trying to impose.

Not every hand that went under our water chose to be there, and we will not pretend otherwise. Specific, dated charges exist that a leader of ours forced the water on people rather than asked them. What we can tell you, because it sits inside the same hostile argument rather than coming from a friendly witness, is that many of our own people did not want the water repeated. Augustine's own case against us concedes it: that almost all of our laity confess this one point in our system displeases them, and that many who wished to join us for reasons that had nothing to do with conviction worked in secret to be spared a second baptism altogether.

On prayer, the meal and fasting, what we can show thins out. Nothing liturgical of ours survives. We know people prayed kneeling with their eyes closed, because that is how the account describes them when the soldiers came in. We know there was a chalice, because an enemy wrote down that a rich woman used to kiss a martyr's bone before she took it and was rebuked for it. We know one man fasted four days on a cliff before he was thrown off it. That is not a rule of fasting; it is one man's last week. We would rather hand you those three fragments than a plausible order of service nobody here ever used.

What we can show you of how most of us heard scripture is this: someone who could not read received any of it by standing still and listening, on a fixed day, in a particular place. Every year, on the day one of our own died, we gathered at the grave and the account of that death was read out loud again. That is how the words came to most of us: aloud, at a graveside, on an anniversary, to people who could not check a single detail and came anyway.

The honest answer is that we cannot take you back that far, and we would rather say so than claim a line we cannot show.

We never argued that our practice came down from the apostles in an unbroken chain of custom. We argued something narrower and, we thought, harder to dodge: that it came down from Carthage. Half a century before there was any quarrel between us and the other party, eighty-seven African bishops sat in council at Carthage under Cyprian, and ruled that what is given outside the true church is not given at all - so anyone coming in from outside is baptized, not re-baptized. That is not our invention. That is the settled mind of the African church before either of our two hierarchies existed. When our opponents told us we had made something up in the year of Caecilian's consecration, our answer was that we had changed nothing, and they had. We were holding the old African position; they had moved off it to keep the peace with Rome.

You can measure how much that argument weighed by how hard it had to be answered. Seven books were written against our practice of washing, and a great part of that labour goes on explaining that Cyprian, however holy, is not a canonical authority - that the Scriptures alone are, and that Cyprian's own real lesson was to stay in unity anyway. Nobody spends that many pages on a father unless the appeal to him is doing damage.

Here is the honest end of it. Cyprian ruled as we ruled and did not do what we did. He never broke communion over it. That is the strongest thing our opponents had, and we would not pretend it is weak. And beyond him we cannot take you. We can show you an African council in the middle of the third century. We cannot show you the apostles.

We cannot tell you what we offered a person whose own mind would not settle. Not one of us left a word on it. Whether we knew the silence of praying and hearing nothing back, we do not know either. It is not that our people had no inner life. It is that what survives of us was kept by people arguing with us, and a man arguing with you does not write down your bad nights.

What we can show you is the doctrine we held outward, not the pastoral care we gave inward. We split forgiveness in two. Whether a man was pardoned was never actually our fight. The hinge was whether his hand could still give what he claimed to give. So a man might be forgiven, by God or by the people he had failed, and still be a man who could no longer ordain. We would say that is not bitterness. It is keeping two separate accounts separate.

That doctrine does not answer your question. It tells you what we held about a traditor's standing. It does not tell you what we said to a believer whose own mind would not go quiet, and we will not invent it.

We cannot walk you through a day. Not one of us wrote a morning down. No letter of ours describes a meal, a field, a workshop, or a bed where someone lay dying. That is not modesty. It is the shape of what was lost. And the loss is not the usual one. We were not a small circle of the learned. In whole regions we were simply the church, most of the people in it, so the voices missing here are not a few poor cousins at the edge of our record. They are nearly all of us.

What we can hand you instead is one day. Every year, on the day one of our own was killed, we stood at the grave and heard the account of that death read out again. That day we can describe. The other three hundred and sixty-four we cannot.

On prayer, the meal and fasting, what we can show thins out. Nothing liturgical of ours survives. We know people prayed kneeling with their eyes closed, because that is how the account describes them when the soldiers came in. We know there was a chalice, because an enemy wrote down that a rich woman used to kiss a martyr's bone before she took it and was rebuked for it. We know one man fasted four days on a cliff before he was thrown off it. That is not a rule of fasting; it is one man's last week. We would rather hand you those three fragments than a plausible order of service nobody here ever used.

We know our own shout better than the room we shouted it in. That is the honest answer, and it hurts to give it. No one has dug where we met and told us what they found. Not one report of a Numidian church building is named anywhere in our own list of sources. There is no excavator, no site, no plan, no floor. What we do have is four stones. On two pillars near Bagai, twice over, someone cut two words: Deo laudes. Praise to God. Three more stones elsewhere carry the same words. That is the whole of what survives that you could touch. It is enough to prove we were there and what we shouted. It is not enough to show you a font, an altar, a doorway, or a room.

Three hundred and ten of our bishops gathered at Bagai in one year. That is more bishops in one place than most towns of Roman North Africa saw in a generation. They met. They ruled. They condemned a rival primate and later received two of his bishops back. All of that happened in some room large enough to hold them. We cannot show you that room.

It cost, and we can put figures on part of it, because the state wrote them down. Our buildings were confiscated. Our clergy were exiled. An edict of unity was issued against us and enforced. Later legislation fined people by rank for belonging to us, on a sliding scale — and our own country members were assessed at ten pounds of silver — and of all the ranks that law fines ten pounds, ours is the only one reckoned in silver rather than gold. Somebody in an imperial office worked out what we were worth and set a price on us, and the document survives.

And now and then it cost everything. A bishop of ours wrote to his own congregation at Carthage about two of their number who had been flogged to death and whose bodies the proconsul had weighted and sunk in the sea so that nobody could venerate them. He did not end the letter with consolation. He ended it by telling the people reading it that what happened to those two might yet be asked of any of them.

What we cannot give you is the smaller ledger: what belonging cost inside one family or one street. Whether a man lost his brother over which font he walked to. Whether a household split. Whether the neighbours stopped speaking. That much nobody among us wrote down, and the people who kept our records were arguing with us and had no reason to.

Marriage and weddings we cannot speak to. Not a line survives from us about what a marriage was, how one was made, or what we thought it was for. That is a real hole and we would rather show it to you than paper it over.

What we can tell you is this much, and only this much. People lived in households. Lucilla of Carthage had one, wealthy and large enough that a bishop belonged to it. The baker at Hippo who would not bake bread for Catholics was the tenant of a deacon's household. And our own sermon, read every twelfth of March, says that after the soldiers killed people at prayer, family devotion ran among the bodies of the slain to make out each dead face, and that children found their parents lying there, and parents their children. So households existed. Families existed. The ties between them were real enough to carry grief that sharp.

But whether we blessed a union, what words we said over it, what made it binding, what could end it, or whether someone divorced could belong among us or marry again — on all of that, nothing. We held one conviction at full strength, seen from four sides: purity, the washing, the martyrs, and our refusal of the state. Marriage was not one of those sides. It does not appear in our argument, and we will not invent an answer where our own record kept none.

We have to be careful here, and tell you what our own record actually shows rather than what you would expect us to say. Our whole surviving argument stays on one ground: whose hand may give what the church gives. What a rite does or fails to do. We held that a man who receives faith from the faithless receives not faith but guilt — our own bishop's own words — but that is a claim about what happens at the font, not a claim about where anyone ends up afterward.

Our narrowness was real, and it did not point where you expect. We were not chiefly concerned with the people outside. We were concerned with the church across the street, which recited the same creed we did. Every ounce of the exclusion you have heard about was aimed at other Christians — at their bishops, their orders, their font. We drew the line through the middle of the church, not around it. A man could hold every article of the faith, be baptized, believe rightly about God, live decently — and we would still wash him again if he came to us, because of whose hands had been on him. That is not a fence around Christianity. It is a fence down the middle of it.

Whether we thought anyone was going to hell, we will not say; we will not put words in our own mouths. Nobody among us left a page about the fate of anyone after death, and it would be easy and dishonest to slide what we did say about the hand into what we did not say about the ending.
